questions.stem: If a small 10% increase in the price of a luxury car leads to a massive 30% drop in its quantity demanded, the demand for this product is considered to be:

options.option_text: Highly Inelastic
Highly Elastic
Unitary Elastic
Perfectly Inelastic

questions.explanation: When the percentage change in quantity demanded is strictly greater than the percentage change in price, the demand is termed 'elastic' (Elasticity > 1). Consumers are highly sensitive to price changes for this good.

questions.stem: Essential life-saving medical drugs, such as insulin for a diabetic patient, typically exhibit what kind of price elasticity of demand?

options.option_text: Highly Elastic
Unitary Elastic
Highly Inelastic
Perfectly Elastic

questions.explanation: Demand for essential life-saving goods is highly inelastic (Elasticity < 1). Even if the price doubles or triples, patients must still buy almost the exact same quantity to survive, as there are no substitutes.

questions.stem: The 'Income elasticity of demand' measures how quantity demanded changes as consumer income changes. For which specific category of economic goods is this value strictly negative?

options.option_text: Normal goods
Luxury goods
Giffen goods
Inferior goods

questions.explanation: For an inferior good, as consumer income increases, they buy LESS of it (because they switch to better quality, more expensive substitutes). Since income goes up and quantity demanded goes down, the income elasticity value is negative. (Giffen goods are a sub-category of inferior goods, but inferior is the broader correct answer).

questions.stem: When the price elasticity of demand for a commodity is exactly equal to unity (|Ed| = 1), what happens to the seller's Total Revenue if the price is increased?

options.option_text: TR increases, as inelastic buyers absorb the price rise without reducing demand
TR falls sharply, as elastic consumers cut demand by more than the price hike
TR stays unchanged, as the percentage drop in demand exactly offsets the price rise
TR rises but at a diminishing rate, reflecting partial consumer adjustment

questions.explanation: C is correct because when |Ed|=1, a 1% price rise causes exactly a 1% fall in quantity, leaving P×Q (Total Revenue) unchanged. Option A is the trap: it describes the outcome when demand is inelastic (|Ed|<1), where TR rises with price. Option B describes elastic demand behaviour, not unitary.

questions.stem: Which of the following characteristics of a good is most likely to make its price elasticity of demand HIGHER (i.e., more elastic)?

options.option_text: The good has a large number of close substitutes available in the market
The good is an essential necessity with very few close substitutes available
Buyers spend only a tiny fraction of their monthly income on this good
Consumers need the good urgently and cannot delay their purchase decision

questions.explanation: A is correct: availability of close substitutes is the primary determinant of high elasticity — consumers switch easily when price rises. Option B (few substitutes, necessity) reduces elasticity. Option C (small income share) also reduces elasticity since consumers don't bother to economise. Option D (urgency) makes demand even more inelastic.

questions.stem: Giffen goods present a paradox in consumer demand theory where their demand curve slopes upward. What is the sign and nature of the price elasticity of demand for a Giffen good?

options.option_text: Negative, because price and quantity always move in opposite directions
Zero, as consumer demand for Giffen goods is completely price insensitive
Negative and greater than 1 in absolute value, making demand highly elastic
Positive, since quantity demanded rises when the price of the good rises

questions.explanation: D is correct: for a Giffen good, price and quantity demanded move in the same direction (income effect dominates substitution effect), giving a positive elasticity value — the defining paradox. Options A and C describe normal goods, where price and quantity move inversely. Option B (zero elasticity) is the trap for students who conflate 'paradox' with 'no response'.

questions.stem: Why is demand for petrol generally MORE price elastic in the long run than in the short run?

options.option_text: Government price controls are stricter in the short run, limiting demand adjustment
Consumers can switch to EVs, carpooling, or public transport given sufficient time
Global crude oil supply becomes less volatile as energy markets mature over time
Rising long-run incomes make consumers more sensitive to small petrol price changes

questions.explanation: B is correct: the adjustment-period effect explains why long-run elasticity exceeds short-run elasticity. In the short run, consumers are locked into existing vehicles and routines. Over time, they can buy fuel-efficient cars, relocate, or shift to public transport. Option D confuses income elasticity with price elasticity — higher income typically reduces price sensitivity, not increases it.

questions.stem: The government imposes a per-unit excise tax on a commodity with highly inelastic demand. Who bears the greater share of this tax burden, and why?

options.option_text: Producers bear most of it, as competition forces them to absorb the tax cost
The tax burden splits equally between buyers and sellers in every market scenario
The government bears the burden indirectly through reduced tax-revenue efficiency
Consumers bear most of it, as they continue to buy nearly the same quantity

questions.explanation: D is correct: tax incidence falls on whichever side adjusts least. Inelastic demand means consumers barely reduce quantity even when price rises, so producers can pass most of the tax forward. Option A (producers bear most) applies when SUPPLY is inelastic, not demand. Option B (equal split) only holds under specific equal-elasticity conditions, not as a general rule.

questions.stem: On a downward-sloping straight-line demand curve drawn on a standard price-quantity diagram, which statement about price elasticity of demand is accurate?

options.option_text: Elasticity equals unity (|Ed|=1) at the exact geometric midpoint of the curve
Elasticity is constant along the entire curve because the slope is constant
Elasticity is highest at the point where the curve crosses the quantity axis
Elasticity increases steadily from the price-axis intercept down to the midpoint

questions.explanation: A is correct: on a linear demand curve, elasticity varies from ∞ at the price-axis intercept, equals 1 at the midpoint, and falls to 0 at the quantity-axis intercept. Option B is the most common error — a constant slope does NOT imply constant elasticity, since the base values of P and Q change continuously. Option C is the opposite of truth: elasticity is 0 (not highest) where the curve meets the quantity axis. Option D is wrong because elasticity actually DECREASES (from ∞ to 1) moving down toward the midpoint.

questions.stem: The Lerner Index of monopoly power is defined as (P – MC)/P, which under profit-maximisation equals 1/|e|. A firm charges ₹150 and its Marginal Cost is ₹100. What is the implied absolute price elasticity of demand the firm faces?

options.option_text: |e| = 2, meaning demand is moderately elastic with price at 1.5× the MC level
|e| = 0.5, indicating inelastic demand — impossible under profit maximisation
|e| = 3, derived from Lerner Index = 50/150 = 1/3, so |e| = 3 by inversion
|e| = 1.5, applying a simple price-to-MC markup ratio as the elasticity value

questions.explanation: C is correct: Lerner Index = (150–100)/150 = 50/150 = 1/3. Setting 1/|e| = 1/3 gives |e| = 3. Option A (|e|=2) is tempting because P/MC = 1.5, but that ratio does not equal elasticity. Option B (|e|=0.5) is a critical conceptual trap: a profit-maximising firm NEVER operates on the inelastic segment of demand (|e|<1), since raising price there would simultaneously increase revenue and lower costs. Option D confuses the markup ratio (1.5) directly with elasticity.
